newsitem.title: JORDAN: IMF head gives Jordan strong confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: IMF head gives Jordan strong confidence vote.

text.p: International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus said Jordan had the fastest growing economy in the Middle East and was on track to accelerate its free-market reforms.

Camdessus was quoted in televised remarks, made during a visit to Jordan this week and broadcast late on Friday, as saying "really dramatic change for the better has occurred" since an economic crisis in 1989 wiped out Jordan's foreign exchange reserves.

He pointed to a drop in the budget deficit to 4.6 percent of GDP in 1996 from 21 percent in 1989 and a fall in the current account deficit to around three percent from 20 percent over the same period.

"Growth was dramatically negative (in 1989)...Now in the last three years you have growth on average of around 6-7 percent, something quite remarkable indeed if you consider that this country has no formidable resources and is developing in a difficult external environment," he said.

Jordan's economy was hard hit by U.N. sanctions imposed on neighbouring Iraq for its invasion of Kuwait seven years ago. Hopes of business with Israel and the Palestinian territories after a 1994 peace accord have failed to materialise, and riots broke out in August when the government cut bread subsidies.
But Camdessus said Jordan had the "highest rate of growth in this part of the world," adding that underlying inflation had fallen to around 3-4 percent from 18 percent in 1989.

"All the key macroeconomic and financial indicators are pointing in the right direction," he said, adding that the government "was totally committed to continue implementing faithfully the arrangement concluded with the IMF."
Jordan embarked last year on a three-year IMF-directed reform to accelerate free market reforms to integrate it into the global economy and expand the private sector role.
He said Jordan had gone beyond conditions set by the IMF.

Jordan was committed to "continue with trade liberalisation, removing distortions in prices, deregulating further the economy and strengthening the environment for the private enterprises to expand and develop freely, to privatise more and more rapidly."

Camdessus warmly endorsed Jordan's efforts to strengthen its social safety net programmes after riots broke out last August in protest against increased prices for bread, a staple food for many of Jordan's 4.2 million population.
The IMF was widely criticised by Jordanians then as being partly responsible for pushing the goverment to take measures which lead to the worst outbreak of civil unrest since 1989.
"The two things, stabilisation reform on one side and improvement in alleviating the conditions of the poor and the most vulnerable are going here hand in hand," he said.
Camdessus said he was recommending to the IMF's executive board "to extend to this country the highest possible support within our limit."
The IMF head also said he would lobby Jordan's Paris Club creditors at their next meeting "to find a generous solution to the problem of debt of this country which remains high."
Last month the finance ministry said Jordan's foreign debt stood at $6.495 billion, or 90 percent of GDP.
